name: Concatenating Strings and Numbers (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that uses variables x, y, and z to print "Python was invented in 1989.".
code:
#Step 1: Assign initial values to the variables x, y, and z
x = "Python was invented in "
y = 1989
z = "."
#Step 2: Print the text using the variables initialized above 
print(x + str(y) + z)

commentList: You assign to variable x the first part of the sentence so you can join it later with the year and the final punctuation.

You use the assignment operator = to store a string literal in x; the text is enclosed in quotes and the trailing space inside the string ensures a space appears between 'in' and the year when you concatenate.
You make x a string value; because y is an integer, you must convert y to a string (as done in Line 6) before using + to concatenate, otherwise Python will raise a TypeError.
If you forget the quotes around the text, Python will treat Python as a variable name and raise a NameError; if you omit the trailing space inside the string you'll get '...in1989' with no space.

For better readability, you should use a clearer variable name than x (for example prefix or sentence_start), and consider using formatted strings (f-strings) or string formatting instead of many + operations.

Note that using print(x, y, z) would let you skip str(y) because print converts non-strings and inserts spaces automatically, but that changes how spacing and punctuation are handled, so choose the approach that gives the exact output you want.

commentList: You assign the integer 1989 to the variable y so the program keeps the year value for later use in the printed message.
You use the = operator to store the value 1989 in the name y. The value 1989 is a numeric integer, so y will hold a number, not text.

If you try to add y directly to a string (for example x + y) Python will raise a TypeError because you cannot concatenate a string and an integer. The code avoids this by converting y to text with str(y) in the print line. A common misconception is that you must put 1989 in quotes; putting it in quotes would make it a string instead of a number, which also works for printing but changes the variable's type.

For clearer code in real programs, use a descriptive name like year instead of y and keep types consistent. When combining numbers and text, either convert the number with str() or use string formatting (for example an f-string) to make the intention obvious.

commentList: You assign the string '.' to z so z holds the final punctuation for the sentence; this lets the print statement build 'Python was invented in 1989.' by joining x, y, and z.
This line uses the assignment operator '=' to store a string literal in z; the period is written inside quotes so Python treats it as text (a str value) rather than code.

Be careful with spacing: x already ends with a space, so you should not include an extra space in z or you'll get two spaces before the period. If you wrote z = . (without quotes) you'd cause a syntax error.

When you concatenate values, all pieces must be strings. In this program y is an int, so the code converts it with str(y) in the print. If you forgot str(y) you'd get a TypeError when trying to add a str and an int.

For clearer code you could use a more descriptive name like 'punctuation' or include the period in x. You might also use an f-string (for example f'{x}{y}{z}') or other formatting, but the simple assignment shown keeps the example easy to follow.

commentList: This line sends the final text to the screen by calling print with a single expression that joins the three variables into one string.

Inside print you use the + operator to concatenate: x + str(y) + z. x is already a string (it includes a trailing space), str(y) turns the number 1989 into the characters '1989', and z adds the final period.
You must convert y to a string with str(y); if you write x + y + z without conversion, Python will raise a TypeError because it cannot concatenate a string and an integer.
A common alternative is print(x, y, z) which avoids the TypeError but inserts spaces between items and uses automatic conversion, so the exact formatting may differ from the intended single sentence.

For clearer and more maintainable code you can prefer an f-string or format method, for example print(f"{x}{y}{z}") or build the full sentence in a single variable before printing; always keep spacing and punctuation explicit so the output matches what you expect.
Remember the order matters: you add x first, then the string form of y, then z, so the pieces appear in the correct sequence to form 'Python was invented in 1989.'

distractors.description: You might pick this because it seems convenient to include the period with the year so the sentence 'looks complete' when you read the assignment. If you use this line while another variable also provides the period, the program will run but the printed sentence will contain two periods (for example, '...1989..'), which is incorrect punctuation. This mistake happens because you placed punctuation inside the year value instead of keeping punctuation in its own variable, leading to duplicated characters in the final string. The result is a visible formatting error even though no runtime error occurs.

You might pick this because it looks like a simple concatenation and you expect Python to join the pieces for you. Step-by-step: you are asking Python to add a string, an integer, and another string with the + operator. Python does not implicitly convert the integer to text for concatenation, so when it tries to evaluate x + y it fails because you cannot add a string and an integer directly. The program will raise a TypeError and stop before printing anything. This distractor misses the required conversion of the numeric variable to text, which is why it is invalid even though it reads like a straightforward concatenation.

You might think this works because you first build the combined text and then tack on the final piece after printing. Step-by-step: Python will evaluate print(x + str(y)) first, which prints something to the screen and returns None. Then the interpreter tries to evaluate None + z, which is invalid and raises a TypeError because None is not a string. The program will either print the first part and then crash, or simply raise an error before finishing. This distractor misunderstands that print does not produce a string value you can continue to concatenate; concatenation must happen before calling print.
